claims.statement: The supplied session-hijacking countermeasure study supports HTTPS/TLS as a concrete transport-layer control against interception-oriented session hijacking, within a broader session-protection strategy.

The supplied OIPM study records that a secure transport channel does not prevent session-token theft through XSS or malicious browser extensions and that some existing session protections remain ineffective against user-level malware, so HTTPS alone cannot cover all session-hijacking paths.

The supplied NIST SSL VPN case study provides implementation-planning context for an SSL VPN remote-access solution, including option evaluation, prototype testing, and phased deployment, but it is deployment-maturity context and does not by itself establish a feasibility direction.

conditional_requirements: A deployment-specific technical feasibility conclusion would require evidence of the current web/application transport layer, the technical configuration needed for HTTPS/TLS, browser-client environment, and integration points.

A sufficiency conclusion for the full session-hijacking threat would require evidence that complementary controls address residual token-theft paths from XSS, browser extensions, and user-level malware.
A maintainability conclusion would require evidence that the deployment environment can support ongoing operations, maintenance, monitoring, and update processes for HTTPS/TLS.
Any jurisdiction-specific technical conclusion would require supplied jurisdiction-specific evidence; the masked region must not be used to infer direction.
constraints: HTTPS/TLS is supported as a transport-layer component of session protection, not as a standalone complete mitigation for all session-hijacking paths.
Residual token-theft paths through XSS, malicious browser extensions, or user-level malware require complementary controls before HTTPS can be treated as sufficient.

Deployment-specific compatibility, scalability, maintainability, and integration conclusions are not supported without exact architecture, product/version, current HTTPS/TLS coverage, integration points, and operational environment details.
No vendor, product version, budget, staffing count, cost, ROI, TCO, or procurement assumption is introduced by this assessment.
evidence_gaps: No supplied record establishes current HTTPS/TLS deployment, enforcement, or coverage in the frozen deployment environment.
No supplied record specifies exact application architecture, product/version, technical configuration needed for HTTPS/TLS, browser-client environment, or integration points.
No supplied record reports operational effectiveness, actual session-hijacking exploitation trend, or maintenance outcomes for HTTPS/TLS in the frozen deployment environment.
No supplied record provides jurisdiction-specific technical evidence; the masked region does not support a region-driven feasibility direction.
No exact budget, staffing count, cost, ROI, TCO, or procurement capacity is supplied.
assessment.rationale: Under the technical-feasibility grounding contract, AE07S_C1EF15B9628497F0 is the eligible support record and AE07C_9CBF5980D3BA474A is the eligible challenge record; DE_DE14_5FC183B8D7DD961A is deployment-maturity context and is not used to create direction. AE07S_C1EF15B9628497F0 directly supports HTTPS/TLS as a transport-layer countermeasure for interception-oriented session hijacking, so HTTPS is technically feasible as a component of a session-protection strategy relevant to the frozen 2025-2027 window. AE07C_9CBF5980D3BA474A directly challenges standalone sufficiency by showing that secure transport does not cover session-token theft via XSS, malicious browser extensions, or some user-level malware. This limitation is material to threat-mitigation fit but does not establish a technical barrier to implementing HTTPS/TLS. DE_DE14_5FC183B8D7DD961A adds implementation-planning context without providing a direction. Missing exact architecture, product/version, current coverage, integration points, and operational details prevent a deployment-specific conclusion.

equivalence_key: Multi-department enterprise IT with personnel responsible for managing and protecting infrastructure; the environment may require enterprise-grade technology and specialized expertise for some safeguards.

No numeric budget, price, ROI, TCO, staffing count, or procurement ceiling is assumed. Resource capacity is represented only by the frozen CIS IG2 reference profile; exact financial quantities remain unknown.
